Claudius. The fourth Roman emperor, who ruled from AD 41 to 54. Afflicted with a limp and slight deafness from a young age, he was largely dismissed by his family as a fool and kept out of public life. However, his physical ailments likely saved him from the purges of his predecessors. Upon Caligula's assassination, he was unexpectedly declared emperor, proving to be an able administrator who oversaw a major expansion of the empire.

He successfully oversaw the Roman conquest of Britain in AD 43, achieving what Julius Caesar and Caligula had failed to do. Following Caligula's murder, he was found cowering behind a curtain by the Praetorian Guard, and they famously proclaimed him emperor on the spot. His third wife, Valeria Messalina, engaged in scandalous affairs and even went through a public marriage ceremony with another man before Claudius had her executed. He was allegedly murdered by his fourth wife, Agrippina the Younger, who was also his niece and who served him a dish of poisoned mushrooms. He was a prolific scholar and historian, famous for writing extensive treatises on Etruscan and Carthaginian history, though these works are now lost.

His erratic nephew Caligula was his predecessor, and Caligula's assassination paved the way for his rise to power. His stepson Nero was his successor, placed on the throne through the machinations of his last wife. Agrippina the Younger was his ambitious niece and final wife, who likely murdered him to secure power for her son.
